claims.text: Intrinsic thermal-expansion-coefficient mismatches among Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr cause the unusual mechanical and thermoelastic behavior of HfNbTaTiZr.
Differential thermal contraction among the constituent elements generates significant internal thermal stresses during cooling.
Cooling-induced internal stresses create local microstrain fields.
Local microstrain fields modulate dislocation mobility.
Cooling-induced strain fields alter phase stability or chemical ordering.
The proposed thermal-stress mechanism jointly governs high-temperature creep, cold-deformation hardening, temperature-dependent elastic properties, and aging hardening.
The initial material is a homogenized, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr alloy with a random elemental distribution.
Rapid quenching from above 1250 °C minimizes development of residual thermal stress.
Slow cooling from above 1250 °C maximizes the buildup of residual thermal stress.
Slow-cooled samples will have higher residual thermal stresses than fast-quenched samples.
Slow-cooled samples will exhibit lower tensile-creep rates at 1250 °C than fast-quenched samples.
After cold rolling, slow-cooled samples will exhibit greater microhardness than fast-quenched samples.
Slow-cooled and fast-quenched samples will exhibit different elastic moduli over 293–1100 K.
Slow-cooled samples will exhibit more pronounced aging hardening at 600–800 °C than fast-quenched samples.
The separate earlier observations qualitatively support a role for thermal stress caused by expansion mismatch.
